en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Mañjuśrī’s Repentance, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha together with a great [assembly].

He was accompanied by a community of monks numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty, and an incalculable number of bodhisattvas—all of whom were great sages who had already attained supernatural powers, acquired dhāraṇīs, grasped the wisdom of the ten directions, established themselves in the three gates of liberation, and understood the three periods of time without obstruction. They proclaimed the Three Jewels to rescue those in the three realms, expounded the three vehicles to bring about the realization of fundamental non-arising and unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, surrounded by a retinue of various bodhisattvas, incalculable great disciples, and gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. For the sake of sentient beings, he extensively expounded the Dharma, elucidating and analyzing it so that they might resolve to train in the three vehicles.
Those who came to listen were originally students of the Śrāvaka vehicle, who inquired of Mañjuśrī concerning the matters of the Four Noble Truths;
those studying the Pratyekabuddha vehicle had already asked about the profound matters of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;

and those studying the Mahāyāna had come from their own practice to inquire about the Six Perfections, the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, and the Great Way of skillful means and infinite expedients.

Some asked about the supernormal powers, the four bases of heedfulness, the four immeasurable mental states, and the various analytical discernments of the Bodhisattva path; some asked about the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the stage of non-retrogression, and the transcendence into nirvana;

some asked about the realms of the buddha-fields, the places for repentance, the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten patiences (*kṣānti*), the ten matters of analytical discernment, the ten auspicious signs, the ten sustainments, the ten seals, and the thirteen samādhis;
and some asked about the indestructibility of all phenomena and the entry into the single principle of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Mañjuśrī answered each according to their questions, gladdening their hearts so that they were left without further doubt.

At that time, there were among the assembly newly initiated bodhisattvas who had come to listen and receive the teaching—those who were unable to guard against the conditions of sin and merit, being shrouded by the *āvaraṇas* (hindrances) and deluded by falsehoods; obscured by uncertainty, habituated to perversion, lacking courageous resolve, relying on physical form and appearance, and harboring timid hearts; such that they could not consult Mañjuśrī to purify all sinful suffering through its causes and conditions, nor to train in the Mahāyāna up to the Unsurpassed Way.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Tathāgatasamaprabhāsaśrī. Seeing that the newly initiated bodhisattvas were hesitant in their thoughts and intentions, unable to resolve them for themselves, he stepped forward and addressed Mañjuśrī regarding the matter of faultlessness, the meaning of repentance, the encouragement of non-failing assistance, the inquiry into being beyond reproach, and the non-contradiction of exhortation and progress.
Mañjuśrī then replied to the Bodhisattva Equal Radiance Illumination as the Tathāgata had instructed:
"It is so, son of good family!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to eliminate sinful karma, practice equanimity, and enter into the Buddha-dharma of the past, future, and present, should prostrate with his five limbs touching the ground, then immediately rise again, place his right knee upon the earth, and speak these words himself:
"All sentient beings follow the left path and cling to the left way; those who dwell in false views shall all be established in the Dharma of the Worthy and Sages.

Desiring to transform all classes of sentient beings so that they may all reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path of equality, for this reason one should kneel with the right knee on the ground and proclaim these words:

"Just as when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha proceeded to the site of enlightenment and sat beneath the Honored Tree, he eliminated all unwholesome dharmas and was universally endowed with all virtues; I, too, am like him."
"Having observed his head and rubbed his entire body with his hand, he again pointed toward the ground with his right hand, saying:
'I shall subdue Māra, along with his retinue.'"
"If I attain the Way of the Buddha, I shall cause all people and the various classes of sentient beings to subdue and eliminate demonic activities and external enemies.

Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he made a solemn vow by pointing to the earth to achieve the holy wisdom of a Buddha, just as the World-Honored One in a former life pointed to the earth with his right hand and subdued eighteen billion demonic officials and their retinues.
For this reason, he pressed his right palm against the ground, and likewise his left hand was placed upon the ground.
Then, kneeling on his left knee, he spoke these words:

"If there be anyone who dwells in the dharma of ignorance, who has undergone perversion and does not accord with the truth, who is stubborn and difficult to transform, who has failed to become a worthy vessel, who is defiled by stinginess and greed, who abides in danger and harm, and who reviles their fellow students—should such a person now recognize the Way, reform their past, cultivate the future, and wholeheartedly receive and practice the four debts of gratitude."
For this reason, he placed his left hand and left knee upon the ground.
When he touched his head to the earth, he uttered these words: "May all people cast away arrogance and pride;

may they be filial toward their parents and reverent toward their elders—providing for them with various kinds of sustenance. May they thereby attain the cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) of a Buddha, whose crown cannot be seen; may they transcend all phenomena of the world, surpass the three realms with their bodies, and exceed the void with their wisdom."
"Now I take refuge; by means of this prostration with the five limbs touching the ground, I pay homage so that all sentient beings may reach the attainment of the Great Way.

"Worldly people grow up under the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*); through this merit, they naturally cast off the obscurations of the five hindrances, become fully endowed with the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), perfect the five powers (*pañcabala*), extinguish the five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), remain far removed from the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and achieve the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*)."

Among the various classes of sentient beings within the five destinies, they have attained the practice of five extraordinary dharmas, distinguished precepts, samādhi, wisdom, the cultivation of liberation, and the matter of transcendent knowledge and vision.

By virtue of this prostration of the five limbs, the veils of obscuration are extinguished; those who abide in the faculties and powers constantly mind the Tathāgata, never letting him depart from their thoughts.

Again, they speak these words: "May all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, graciously bestow compassion and look upon us with pity. Thus, all Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, up to the Buddhas themselves, possess wisdom free from obstruction and practice non-duality. In this state of equality, they protect the marks of the Dharma; through the pure words of the Dharmakāya, there is no conceptual explanation, and with a pristine mind, they are yet without a mind.

All dharmas are characterized by wisdom that is free from obscuration; they neither come nor go. With universal compassion, one perceives all-knowledge, equally entering into the essential meaning of the Tathāgata’s realization regarding the dharmas of the past, future, and present.

Knowing the retribution of the causes and conditions of both transgressions and blessings, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess the sacred eye; their wisdom is perfected such that they can fully testify to these matters, having prepared themselves with diligent effort for the great responsibility of serving as guides for humanity.

From the beginningless limit until the present cycle of birth and death, I have been deluded regarding the limit of ultimate truth; unable to attain swift penetration or possess any true knowledge, I dwelt amidst what is not the Dharma while conceiving the notion that it is the Dharma, transgressed the regulations while conceiving the notion that they were regulations, regarded those who are not the Protectors as the Protectors, and gave rise to unwholesome states while conceiving the notion that they were wholesome.

The mind follows after perversions, failing to understand impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; it greedily clings to the view of a self and commits various evil and sinful deeds, acting contrary to the Dharma and violating the prohibitions and restrictions established by the Buddha.

"Whether I have committed these offenses myself or incited others to do so—namely, the coverings of sin and the afflictions that prevent hearing the Dharma, the karma of harboring hatred toward Bodhisattvas and the noble assembly, failing to uphold the Way and its teachings, encountering various demonic deeds, distancing oneself from the *pāramitās* and the various infinite perfections, obstructing others from practicing giving, and destroying the roots of virtue in others so they cannot achieve fulfillment—I now, before the radiant light of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, repent and confess all of this. I dare not conceal it, so that its calamities may be removed, and I shall reform my past and cultivate my future."

"From this day forward, we dare not commit such transgressions again. Do not let us be burdened by the coverings of various sins, nor fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or spirits, nor suffer poverty. If we are among humans, do not let us be destitute; if we are in the heavens, do not let us be poor devas. May we be broad-minded and proficient in the various sutras rather than impoverished in the Way; may our wealth and resources be abundant rather than stricken by want, so that we may provide the seven treasures of Dharma for those of little wisdom."
The hindrances of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind invade one's kin and cause the destruction of the conditions of the heart.
If one is born in a remote region, family members will engage in strife and become separated from one another, amidst foul odors, defects, and impurities that are unbearable.
May I never again associate with such a retinue, but always meet and see together with those true men who act in accordance with the Way.
I now repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions, reforming my past ways and cultivating myself for the future, not daring to conceal anything.
Mañjuśrī said: "One should further reproach oneself:

'In my previous lives, my conduct was impure; I violated my body, speech, and mind. Lust, anger, and delusion arose in my heart to do harm; I practiced negligence, flattery, and deceit; I was insatiable in my many desires; I accumulated evil karma; I slandered and treated with contempt the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; I was unfilial toward my parents; and I held my elders and superiors in disdain.'"

Ordinary people, obscured by the merit of the World-Honored One, are unable to awaken to their own state; they disparage the sages with their meager intellects, praising themselves while seeking out the faults of others. Having committed transgressions themselves, they further incite others to do the same, and those who follow their lead they instruct to overstep the Dharma.

They do not know the proper time for the Buddha, the proper time for the Dharma, the proper time for the Saṅgha, nor the proper time for good and evil; they are deeply submerged and obstructed by greed, lust, and hatred, shrouded by ignorance such that they cannot exert diligence, being envious, insincere, fierce, and difficult to transform.

With many aspirations and attachments, calculating and grasping at a self, they dwell upon the lifespans of others and give rise to thoughts of the five destinies; through seeking and amassing, they harbor thoughts of flattery and accumulate limitless unrighteous deeds.
One reckons that there is a self, conceives of things as "mine," and perceives the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure.

Falling into the four inversions, they plant evil karma; they are intoxicated by physical form and appearance, deluded by wealth and occupation, confused by pride and nobility, distracted by national rank, and disordered in their kinship.

Regarding the transgressions and offenses committed—having seen the Buddhas yet being unwilling to inquire or receive their teachings, having failed to make offerings to the Sangha, having abandoned the roots of virtue, having forsaken the *pāramitās* and forgotten the mind of enlightenment, having violated and lost the Three Jewels, and furthermore, having discarded inexhaustible right action, immeasurable merit, and the inexhaustible sagely wisdom and eloquence; having indulged in one's own desires, following evil associates and remaining distant from virtuous friends—I now confess these before the Buddhas of the ten directions, reforming my past and cultivating the future, not daring to conceal anything.
Mañjuśrī spoke again: "One should repent, saying: 'In my past lives, my aspirations were base and inferior;

in the lands where I wandered, I made vows to disparage the Mahāyāna, obstruct the True Teaching, encourage others to follow deviant paths, and slander the sublime and profound scriptures proclaimed by the Buddha. Through various kinds of teachings, I suppressed the Wheel of Dharma so that it could not flow freely.'"
Whether one commits these acts oneself or instructs others to do so—such as encouraging and assisting in unrighteousness; destroying stupas and monasteries; causing disorder among the noble assembly;
dispersing towns and villages; ruining great kingdoms; endangering cities and districts; plotting against the sovereign; harming members of one's own clan or relatives, both internal and external;
or further maiming and injuring the bodies of others, causing them to bear scars and wounds, and threatening their very life-force; [in all such cases...]
To imprison someone in a dungeon, or to incite others to kill;

to have a deluded and distracted mind, constantly harboring doubt; to incite others to hesitation, to speak of their sins and calamities, causing them to disobey the precepts and dwell in false views; to follow heterodox teachings and turn away from right practice;
to harbor resentment within oneself, to disturb the minds of others, and to cause them to become inevitably angry.

Regarding all transgressions committed—whether personally perpetrated by myself or instigated in others—I confess and repent for them all before the Buddhas of the ten directions. May I receive the illumination of the World-Honored Ones and be granted their salvation; I shall reform my past ways and cultivate myself for the future, never again daring to conceal my faults.
Mañjuśrī said: "One should further repent and say:
'In my former reckoning, I conceived of a self and claimed things as mine; my perceptions were inverted, and I dwelt in lustful desire.'"
The mind has no fundamental basis, yet one imagines it possesses a mind; one cannot clearly understand that the mind is like a magical illusion, for its nature is spontaneous.

Unable to discern the teachings of the Buddhas, one fails to give rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment, yet still desires to perceive the location where the Way resides.
All dharmas are entirely non-existent, yet one conversely says they exist.

Regarding the good and evil deeds performed by body, speech, and mind, one confesses them from the very beginning before the radiant light of the worlds of the ten directions, reforming the past and cultivating the future, not daring to conceal anything.
"In the past, when I practiced giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, I did not understand samādhi and remained in inverted views."

If one practices giving while falsely imagining a reward, observes the precepts with a mind intent on grasping, cultivates patience while conceiving of self and others, maintains diligence by clinging to the body, enters meditative concentration while dwelling in manifold conceptualizations, contemplates what is appropriate and inappropriate while imagining the existence of persons, delights in negligence while greedily seeking wisdom, or aspires to the Path while believing there is a fixed location—all such faults are confessed before the Light of the Worlds of the ten directions; one reforms the past and cultivates the future, not daring to conceal anything.

"In the past, I was unable to comprehend the meaning of the true and correct Dharma and failed to make offerings to the Buddha; instead, I relied upon and sought after physical marks and the eighty minor signs of excellence."

Although they serve the Buddha, they are unable to enter the dharma-realm of indestructible phenomena, nor do they understand the phenomena of non-abiding; instead, they dwell upon various conceptualizations of phenomena.

Should they hear the Dharma of the sutras or listen to its exposition, they contemplate the goal toward which it leads, yet do not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharma. They reckon upon the assembly of noble ones with a sense of numerical limitation, and even in making offerings to the noble ones, they give rise to expectations. From all directions, they repent before the Light of the World, reforming their past ways and cultivating themselves for the future, never daring to conceal their faults.

"In the past, I aspired to all dharmas and sought the state of emptiness; I dwelt in seclusion, observed moderation and contentment, and took few desires as my virtue. Yet, I was unable to realize that all dharmas are empty and that the mind has no attachments. Only when one can do so may it be said that one is sitting in tranquility in a quiet place, abiding in the Dharma-realm."

They are unable to comprehend that the dharma-realm is without reception, nor that the realm of sentient beings is likewise without reception; furthermore, by relying on a self and establishing perverse attachments, they sink into delusion and are unable to practice the Path.

Furthermore, one calculates that there are those who do not cultivate the four debts of gratitude; though they intend to save sentient beings, they cannot bring them relief. They do not understand the natural characteristics of the Buddha-way, nor do they realize that within the dharmas of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, there is naturally no "I" arising upon which to rely or from which to seek hope. Thus, they do not know the meaning of the silent śramaṇa.

Having gone forth, one cultivates and receives the full precepts and conducts oneself according to the practice of a bhikṣu; through such deeds and other roots of merit thus created, one attains peace and security by virtue of those roots of merit.

The merit of conditioned phenomena and the peace of the unconditioned are vastly separated and far removed; they do not accord with the Way. One must repent before the light of the worlds of the ten directions, reforming the past and cultivating the future, never daring to conceal one's faults.
"Just as the Buddhas of the past, the Gods among Gods, when they were originally practicing the path as Bodhisattvas, all repented of their sins, hindrances, and obscurations, so shall I do;
and just as the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the future and the present have originally amended their faults, I now repent of my transgressions in the same manner."

I turn toward the Honored One, confessing my transgressions and taking refuge in the Buddha—He who is supreme, the eldest, the most excellent and extraordinary, the unsurpassed one of peerless virtue; whose noble wisdom is majestic and immeasurable, who fully knows the number of every mote of dust in all worlds and has attained mastery therein, and who universally understands the thoughts and intentions of all sentient beings.
Throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, our bodies have wandered in delusion and been self-indulgent; we now repent for all our transgressions and the afflictions of the *skandhas*.

Just as I repent for the calamities and transgressions committed by my own self, so too do I now, with my five limbs prostrate, take upon myself and repent for all the sins that shroud those sentient beings within the five destinies—those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.
"Having clearly understood the subtle and wondrous, and having eliminated all limitations and obstructions, one is already able to enter the contemplation of all phenomena.
It is like empty space: that which is repented of has no offense, no retribution, and no defilement."
One who has already entered into all dharmas and is free from the veil of transgression is said to be "repenting of all faults. Thus, noble son!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva must repent for all past fetters, all mental activities and delusive thoughts, the causes and conditions of wealth and livelihood, and the places of dwelling upon which they have relied and depended.
If, within this state, one’s perceptions, thoughts, and mental formations regarding such forms and appearances are unequal, one must clearly realize that they are all fundamentally without basis.

Should one be such that there is nothing at all being performed, then one is able to enter this limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*): the limit of non-conceptualization, the limit of formlessness, the limit of non-duality, the limit of the absence of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), the limit of non-attainment, the limit of bodilessness, the limit of freedom from desire, the limit of non-practice, the limit of non-action, the limit of non-obstruction, the limit of nowhere to return, and the limit of nowhere to proceed. This is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s confession from the very beginning—being free from the harm of transgressions, attaining the wisdom of a Buddha, and extinguishing all weariness, calamities, obstructions, and veils.

Mañjuśrī said: “Having repented for all these transgressions and offenses, one should immediately resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). One should pray to eliminate all calamities and misfortunes for the sake of all classes of sentient beings, to cause them to be free from the veil of sin, and to enable them to become Buddhas of right and true enlightenment within this world; do not [aim for] the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

To transform and enlighten sentient beings: those who seek deliverance, I shall deliver them; those who are not yet liberated, I shall liberate them; those who seek parinirvāṇa, I shall lead them to parinirvāṇa; I shall be a dwelling place of salvation for all people.

He protects those who take refuge, guides and shows them the path, and follows the Lamp of Wisdom; with the radiance of his light, he serves as the leader, the merchant, and the great guide for the multitude.

By means of these ten powers of the Tathāgata, in the mere instant of conceiving the thought [of awakening], they cause one to attain the adornments of the four fearlessnesses, the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty secondary characteristics, and the eightfold resonance of the Tathāgata’s voice; they clearly recognize the Tathāgata’s skillful means and enter the minds of sentient beings.
"The Buddha’s vast and supreme great wisdom resides within the dharma-realm; his precepts are pure and without flaw, as he rains down the vajra verses of all dharmas."
By not abandoning any class of sentient beings, one does not regress, ultimately attaining all-knowledge and the wisdom of the superknowledges, and giving rise to the true, upright mind.

They are without attachment to any of the Buddha-dharmas, and by means of the roots of virtue, they encourage and assist all Buddhas—those of the past, future, and present—in their original practices and training on the path.

From the first aspiration until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment as a most perfectly awakened one, throughout this interval, the roots of virtue manifested are, as taught by the Buddha, such that all dharmas have no root-source and no place of abiding.
"In that which is given up, there is nothing given;
its intrinsic nature is pure, and because the precepts are pristine and stainless, there is no transgression;
when all sentient beings are exhausted [of grasping], there is no arising—this is called patience."
Silent stillness and non-action constitute diligence;
the mind being spontaneous and without arising constitutes single-mindedness;
saving without one to save, not crossing over turbulent waters, and abandoning all false views constitute wisdom.
"To enter into the profound twelvefold dependent origination while having nothing to enter is what can be called 'mysterious and wondrous.
To clearly realize the emptiness of conditioned formations is 'loving-kindness.
To perform that which is non-performing is called 'compassion.'"
Not engaging in any phenomena is called "joy";
to transcend the four great rivers without duality is called "protection";
being without receiving or non-receiving, and likewise without anything grasped, constitutes the "fourfold kindness."
To have no root and no place of abiding is the foundation of virtue; this is called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
For the mind to have no thoughts and no wandering is the five powers (*pañcabala*).
To fully awaken to and comprehend all truths, from their beginning to their end, constitutes the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
To be non-conforming with duality, without conjunction or dispersion—this is called the Way (*dharma*).
To attain suchness through the practice of serenity—this is called tranquility (*śamatha*).
To cross over by means of liberating wisdom without violating gentleness and compliance—this is called insight (*vipaśyanā*).
To take wisdom as one’s companion is called supernatural power (*abhijñā*).
I exhort and assist all beings with this to lead them toward the wheel of non-retrogression, guiding them equally until they reach Buddhahood.

For this reason, the Tathāgata, having fully adorned and perfected his body, expounds these meanings through written words and speech; he provides analytical explanations according to the languages and sounds of all sentient beings, such that his proclamations are everywhere pervasive and cannot be suppressed.

Therefore, the Tathāgata always attains mastery over the ten powers; adorned with wisdom, he achieves perfection, manifesting all the transformations of the Buddhas—unsurpassed, infinite, most honored, incomparable, and peerless.
I exhort and assist all such practices of the Dharma.
Regarding the fundamentally pure bodies of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones—past, future, and present—one understands that they are spontaneously non-apprehensible.
What is called "purity" is such that even the purity of the mind cannot be apprehended, for there is nothing to be sent forth.
To make offerings to all Buddhas while not guarding or protecting any phenomena is itself the protection of the Dharma; therein is neither merit nor an assembly.
To make offerings to the Sangha, they have fully prepared all majestic deportment and ritual propriety, and have likewise accomplished all practices.
Their conduct being thus, together with other matters, they understand that the wisdom of the path of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present is equal.

“Practicing the Buddha-dharma with equanimity, one does not err by falling into the realm of any demons; one does not become defiled by sharing the same dust as all worldly dharmas; one does not cling to the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; one cuts off all that is non-virtuous, honors the perfections (pāramitās), and attains dhāraṇī.”

Cultivating the bodhisattva practices, they quickly draw near to the Way; they are able to respond to everything said by sentient beings, freely following whatever each person desires to inquire about, so that all may find their proper place.

Ever-abiding and impartial, their conduct is self-directed; they adorn all Buddha-lands, and their radiant eloquence returns to purity. They sever all evil destinies and attain mastery over samādhi, acting at will according to the needs of all sentient beings. Having attained all dhāraṇīs, there is nothing they do not illuminate; their sagely eloquence and penetration shall all proceed from themselves.
Thus, with the mind of omniscience that has been generated, one should entirely employ it to encourage and assist the wisdom of the path of all Buddhas.

Regarding those of the past, future, and present who have attained the Buddha-way—being free from all outflows (*āsrava*), and possessing the matters of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; they roam through the various powers (*bala*) without being able to regress, relying upon the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*).
The Dharma of all Buddhas is free from all obstructions; their practice of infinite compassion is peerless, and those who possess great pity do not look up to others for support.

Equal as space, they are unable to be scrutinized at the crown of their heads; they possess no dualistic marks of karmic retribution, and having purified and eliminated the deluded mind, they adorn themselves in body, speech, and mind.

The various devas, Śakra, and Brahmā have all come to offer their encouragement and assistance; you shall expound the Way of the Buddhas and turn the Wheel of Dharma, casting aside ignorance and lack of understanding regarding the spiritual consciousness, transforming all sentient beings to establish them in the Buddha-wisdom, and I shall provide all encouragement so that they may reach the unsurpassed Great Way of Buddhahood.

"When there are Buddhas of the past, future, and present who, at the time of their final passing into parinirvāṇa, employ skillful means and establish themselves through majestic spiritual power to disseminate their relics so that people may make offerings to them."

I shall embrace the dispositions and natures of all sentient beings from beginning to end, until even the extinction of the True Dharma; I will exhort and assist all those who may be exhorted and assisted, directing their will toward the unsurpassed Great Way of the Buddha’s wisdom.

“The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, manifesting their parinirvāṇa, assemble the śrāvakas; they transcend all hindrances and guide those of sincere faith to understand the flavor of the dharma-realm. They guide them through mindfulness of the Dharma to cross beyond the eight heterodoxies, which are known as the eightfold path.”
Abiding on the ground of the unconditioned lineage, those of that lineage are numerous; by reversing their flow, they become *srotāpannas*;
by returning twice and revolving [in saṃsāra], they become *sakṛdāgāmins*;
by passing away from this life and being born there, no longer returning, they become *anāgāmins*.
Those who are unconditioned, without arising, and have nothing further to advance toward are Arhats;
those who analytically understand and clearly comprehend the profound and subtle twelvefold dependent origination are Pratyekabuddhas;
and those whose vision perceives all things and whose wisdom reaches everywhere are the Bodhisattvas.
"The mind of one who has first resolved to attain enlightenment is equal to the earth, universally entering into all practices.

Their practice of the ultimate truth exhausts the source of all phenomena within birth and death; being fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma, they become non-retrogressive. Being unborn amidst all births, they are then able to reach the stage of the single-birth-to-Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha)."

I expound and proclaim the wisdom of non-existence, radiating a great light; I fully encourage and assist such a Dharma as this, wherein all roots of virtue are entirely without root and have no place of abiding.

"Those who set their will upon the unsurpassed Great Way of the Buddha’s wisdom, throughout the three periods of past, future, and present, shall purify the Buddha-eye among all classes of sentient beings."
In whatever they give as alms, they do not conceive of a self and harbor no craving or attachment;
the merit they cultivate through their observance of precepts is inexhaustible and immeasurable.

In the practice of the Way and its principles, their conduct is non-conduct; all their merits they dedicate toward assisting the wisdom of all Buddhas. In the Unsurpassed Great Way, there is no differentiation; it is equal and without diminution, pure and free from defilement, just like empty space.

Entering into the assembly of noble ones of sublime wisdom, one becomes the supreme guide for the multitude of meanings; through diligent practice of the Dharma, it is naturally like space—true and peerless—and like the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it has no companion. It is by means of this that one provides encouragement and assistance.
"To state the essentials:

Just as the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, when they were originally Bodhisattvas seeking the Way, practiced immeasurable deeds, the Perfection of Wisdom, skillful means, and unimpededness; and having thoroughly cultivated and purified their true practice, attained the Buddha-wisdom upon completing those pure deeds—so too should one now assist and encourage the very foundations of all these manifold virtues."

"I shall study this honored Dharma-practice and provide assistance therein, setting my mind upon the unsurpassed Great Way of Buddha-wisdom, so that all sentient beings—equal in number to the atoms filling the worlds of the ten directions—may, in all their physical actions, behold the Buddha and cause them all to resolve their minds toward enlightenment beyond measure, understanding the Great Way and attaining mastery in their conduct."
I fully exhort and assist these roots of merit.
One must realize that these roots of merit cannot be grasped or maintained, for all phenomena are like empty space.
If one can thus exhort and assist these roots of merit, then there will be no root at all.
Having already transcended all roots [of existence] that cannot be maintained, one is without volition or thought, being tranquil and unborn;
having realized non-arising, one enters into all phenomena (*dharmas*);

having entered into all phenomena, one then encourages the roots of virtue. Just as one encourages and assists oneself, one likewise encourages and assists all bodhisattvas, and transforms sentient beings in exactly the same way, without any distinction or difference.
It is so, son of good family!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva encourages and assists the Buddha-wisdom, following it without error until reaching the Great Way.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in such profound and wondrous great meaning, yet he further proclaims these words of teaching:

"There are in the ten directions incalculable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who in their respective worlds have attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and realized supreme perfect enlightenment; they have thoroughly understood the sutras, transcended the four māras, and attained the dharma of non-attainment and tranquility, which is entirely free from words and letters and accords with the two matters of the sages."

They further contemplate the Dharma they have attained, manifesting the reception of the Dharma through skillful means to transform and deliver those sentient beings who are ready to be saved, never failing in their great compassion.

I prostrate myself and inquire: Delighting in profound stillness, you contemplate that Buddha-tree, which is praised by devas, nāgas, spirits, and gandharvas; you fully comprehend all sounds, languages, and expressions, and preach for the sake of all beings.

If one establishes this practice, one will be able to subdue Māra and his retinue, and transform all enemies so that they become free of thorns—what are called "thorns" refers to the three poisons—one will fulfill all aspirations, immediately eliminate all obscurations and darkness as intended, and thus become a boundlessly great radiance for the world.

“The radiance of their noble wisdom enters the immeasurable; they are discerning and sagacious, with no path to which they do not have access. Their wheel of wisdom cannot be obstructed or destroyed; they employ skillful means to thoroughly understand the fundamental nature of all sentient beings. In preaching the Dharma for them, nothing can restrain them, as they sever all fetters and obstructions in every place, illuminating what the multitudes desire to inquire about and receive.”

"Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, I bow my head to all Buddhas, reverently taking refuge in them as supreme, extraordinary, foremost, peerless, unsurpassed, incomparable, and beyond match; for the wisdom of the Buddha is thus difficult to attain, observing the non-dual limit."
My prostration in this manner is truly a prostration to the Buddha; he is neither born from anywhere nor does he go anywhere.

By prostrating with patience at my head to repent for calamities and transgressions, and by bowing my head to the Buddha to repent and take refuge, my misfortunes and sins are extinguished and eliminated, like clouds dispersing when the sun rises.

"Suppose there were as many classes of sentient beings as the dust motes filling all the infinite worlds of the ten directions; in the mere moment of generating the resolve for enlightenment, they would utter words and contemplate inconceivable numbers of thoughts, exhorting and assisting all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma."
"These World-Honored Ones turn the unsurpassed wheel, the non-dual wheel, the formless and unconditioned wheel,
the wheel that is ungraspable, the wheel that tears asunder all the nets of Māra, and the wheel that,
having long ago awakened to the non-arising of phenomena and attained the Great Way, rises up; they transform and enlighten sentient beings and adorn [the world]."
The wheel that purifies the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; the wheel of entry into the path that possesses invincible power through the great subduing of all [obstacles] toward omniscience;
the wheel of understanding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the wheel of non-action, as well as the wheel of neither arising nor origination;
and the wheel of ultimate truth wherein nothing at all exists—all these are to be accomplished.
The wheel that achieves nothing [in terms of self], the wheel that can subdue yet has nothing to deliver,
the wheel of profound and subtle understanding of the twelve links of dependent origination, the wheel that destroys all Māras and repels external enemies;
it eliminates delusion, harm, and hostile thieves, beats the unassailable drum of the infinite Dharma, and likewise blows the conch of the...
To speak of the Dharma-conch is likewise to erect the banner of the wisdom of the Dharma.

Furthermore, with the great brilliance of the liberation of noble wisdom, one kindles a blazing, infinite torch; immediately thereafter, one rains down immeasurable ambrosia. The water-drops of this Dharma delight the sentient beings and the wisdom of the worthy and sages, and they satisfy them with the unsurpassed Great Way through the seven factors of enlightenment. Thus, one extinguishes the roots and sprouts of all classes of sentient beings—the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, distress, and the obstructions of the web of fetters—as well as the dense darkness of ignorance. Therefore, it is said that by kindling the infinite great lamp of the light of wisdom, one manifests and explains for each being the fruits of their respective karmic actions, whether of transgression or merit.

"These World-Honored Ones, existing in countless and incalculable assemblies throughout the worlds of the ten directions, perform the Buddha-work, skillfully demonstrating the Dharma and Vinaya, never interrupting their verbal teachings, and discerning with precise wisdom."

Furthermore, they bestow predictions of enlightenment upon all bodhisattvas; they remain steadfastly established within the noble assembly, transforming and enlightening sentient beings; they seek the profound, wondrous, tranquil, and unconditioned state, receiving and upholding the sutras without ever feeling weary or satisfied.

"When the Great Sages, the Buddhas, desire to enter parinirvāṇa, I shall exhort and assist them all so that they do not pass into extinction; with single-minded devotion, their conduct shall be peaceful and secure, abiding in accordance with the dharma-realm and existing eternally."

For incalculable, countless, and immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they have taught and transformed sentient beings; abiding in the six *pāramitās*, they deliver all without exception, never abandoning a single person until they are saved, universally causing them to enter the gates of all *dhāraṇīs*, so that all may perceive the beginning of the causal practices of the samādhis of all Buddhas.

"If one plants the seeds of Right Dharma and establishes oneself in Great Samādhi, encouraging the aspiration for the Mahāyāna, one shall be sent to all Buddha-worlds to manifest that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, attain perfect enlightenment from the state of non-arising;
they manifest birth while in reality there is no birth, and their non-extinction is likewise such that there is extinction, being naturally quiescent and entirely free from attachment."
"This, noble son, is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva encourages and assists the Buddha-wisdom without incurring any fault or transgression. Mañjuśrī said:

"Having been able to repent in this manner for the transgressions you have committed, you should now resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, always directing a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and harboring no resentment or enmity."
Being free from resentment, one invites the deities of the three realms and encourages all that is the root of merit.

Bowing one’s head to all Buddhas and taking refuge in them, one repents of transgressions, exhorts the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and manifests the immeasurable virtues established therein; thus, one shall give rise to the wisdom of *sarvajñā* (all-encompassing knowledge) and all the swift and penetrating insights.

"In the worlds of the ten directions, there are rare and extraordinary treasures to which no one has claim—flower garlands, various incenses, powdered incenses, unguents, lamps, robes, banners, canopies, and silken streamers; musical instruments that sound spontaneously without being struck; palaces, bathing pools, rivers, seas, springs, and sources; and the radiance of the sun and moon—none of which have a sovereign, nor is anyone even bold enough to claim them. With my own eyes I see these, and with my mind I take them, to offer as tribute to the Buddhas, the World-Illuminators, the Gods among Gods. With this abundance of wondrous jewels and rare treasures, I shall serve all the Buddhas."

All the seven-jeweled trees, naturally exquisite flowers and incense, celestial music, and couches and beds found within the heavens and the world of the three realms, he further offered to the Buddhas above.

"Having completed the offerings, they clearly understand that all Buddhas are identical and equal; that all Buddhas are non-dual and without form, yet manifest the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, displaying infinite colors through skillful means."
Whatever he proclaims, his voice is heard afar;
he manifests countless bodies in incalculable forms.

He dwells nowhere within the various worlds, yet does not abide in the dharma-realm as he cherishes sincerity and faith. Through the liberation of causes and conditions, he offers what is worthy of worship, honoring the Buddhas with the virtue of service.

"These World-Honored Ones do not waver within the realm of all phenomena (dharmadhātu); they do not apprehend any location for the perfections (pāramitās), yet they enter into non-obstruction, reaching the ultimate limit."
One should examine the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings as being like a vast wilderness—devoid of a master and entirely non-existent.
Failing to understand this, one needlessly undergoes suffering and affliction.

Transforming the various classes of sentient beings, they resolve their will upon *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and the wisdom of the superknowledges; universally entering all practices, they attain the body of a Tathāgata, and in all practices they enter, they completely relinquish both existence and non-existence.
They manifest the realms of sentient beings and humans to eliminate arrogance;
they turn the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma without negligence, abandon all frivolity, and subdue the various māras.
The dispositions and natures of sentient beings are immeasurable; by severing their sensory faculties, he manifests the infinite.
All sentient beings dwell within various nets of entanglement, yet through the power of the Way, he extensively reveals their true meaning.

In matters of equality, there are no hindrances or obscurations, and from the very beginning, they are also unshakable; they fully manifest and proclaim the universal gate, becoming complete in the attainment of *sarvajñā* wisdom, and purify the meritorious virtues of all Buddhas to adorn their bodies.

“By making offerings to the relics with these lamps, incense, various flowers, diverse fragrances, and all manner of ritual implements—the merit of such manifold nourishment—I present them to the Buddhas, the lights of the world:
‘Just as the Bodhisattvas of the past Buddhas made offerings in various ways, their minds free from attachment as they presented them to the Buddhas;
may I likewise establish this supportive offering. May the Great Sages, out of great compassion, look upon me with pity and graciously accept it.’”
Mañjuśrī said: "Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in such a manner, he should speak these words:"

"The transgressions for which I repent are empty and unreal; that which may be encouraged and assisted likewise has no arising; that which may be inquired about is also non-existent. Calculating this, what I have repented of is empty and lacks reality."
"If that which I have exhorted is non-arising, and that which may be inquired about is likewise non-existent, then the Way is also thus—empty and non-existent.
"That which is non-arising and non-existent is equal and fixed; it is likewise such that there is no arising."
There is no one who crosses over; there is no attachment and no thought. Having no attachments, one is then able to believe in liberation.

Through the encouragement of non-attachment, the categories of merit from the foremost repentance of transgressions are reckoned as the mind of the Way, whereby all sentient beings attain mastery over the absence of both sin and merit.

All that we have encouraged and assisted was for the purpose of making offerings to the assembly of all Tathāgatas with the roots of virtue; we prostrate and take refuge, presenting lamps, incense, flowers, canopies, necklaces, and various other kinds of objects.
Regarding those who make offerings, they take these merits and make them all into a single flavor of pure conduct—what is purified is the naturally pure, fresh, clean, and radiant intrinsic nature.

Taking equal universal wisdom as the practice of the great and infinite gift, practicing the path with benevolence, harmony, and stainlessness, one shall gather all aspirations so that they lead toward the way of the Tathāgata; thus, one encourages and assists others toward unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment as the most supreme awakening.
"All dharmas are without mutual encouragement or assistance:

even if the eye does not encourage form, one understands that form is natural and is not attached to by the eye; the retribution of causes and conditions is reckoned according to its consciousness. That which arises does not emerge from the eye, nor is there any such thing as form; as soon as it arises, it perishes and is destroyed, dissolving and vanishing until nothing remains, having no place of abiding.

It is the same for the ear and sound, the nose and fragrance, the tongue and flavor, the body and touch, and the mind and mental objects—there is no dharma that can encourage them, for the mind has no such dharma."
"All merits are likewise thus: they encourage and assist the Way, yet the Way has no root of merit.

There are causes and conditions that arise from the root of merit, and the mind is aroused because of one's practice; yet the mind of the Way that is generated has no place of abiding—it arises and immediately perishes, dissolving and vanishing away."
"He creates the roots of virtue with his mind; that which he employs to encourage and assist practitioners is a succession of mental states that do not perceive one another.

It is like a lamp or the light of the sun during the day: it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; as soon as it arises and produces its flame, it is formed by the conjunction of causes and conditions, yet suddenly one knows not where it is.
The Bodhisattva’s path-mind is also like this: the brilliance of wisdom gives rise to and manifests the roots of virtue, yet it has no dwelling place."

One who is thus born through the Dharma is said to be a bodhisattva who encourages others to enter into tranquility, receives the prediction of enlightenment, attains patience, and reaches the radiant splendor of noble wisdom.

"If a bodhisattva dwells within this Dharma and their mind takes no pleasure in practicing the source of all defilements, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, shall bear witness; only then should they encourage and assist others to resolve upon the roots of virtue."

Just as the Buddhas possess the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, and through their noble insight cause all bodhisattvas to practice right virtue, so too do I remain unshakable in my exhortations and assistance.
With such diligence, their Way reaches everywhere, encompassing all things without exception.
"In accordance with the power of their resolute nature, they enter into the immeasurable, and they likewise cast away all conceptual thoughts regarding what is appropriate and what is inappropriate."
If one has already attained entry into the nature of the assembly of practitioners, they should contemplate all Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones, as being present before them;
they should contemplate space, such that all that exists is equal to emptiness.
Having attained contentment of mind, they enter the immeasurable and fully accomplish all practices within the dharma-realm.

With the wisdom of supernormal powers, they ascend the Hall of Sovereignty; thereupon, they are able to articulate their realization and manifest their minds, universally casting off the defilements of the world, tearing asunder the net of ignorance, and entering into self-restraint.
They all behold the Buddhas of the ten directions—the Gods among Gods—and the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, without leaving anyone out or failing to see them.
Contemplating that the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are all of one and the same kind, they then encourage and assist noble wisdom by means of their roots of virtue.
“I now offer my encouragement and assistance so that it may reach all beings throughout the two realms without exception;
this root of virtue is likewise such that it shall cause all to be universally pervaded.

It shall be extended to all living beings, enabling them all to enter every vehicle and the ground born from the gateways of all Bodhisattvas, so that they may fully attain perfection and none fail to behold and contemplate it.”
They cause their visual faculty to see all sentient beings, ultimately and completely mastering immeasurable Buddha-activities.

They cause everything within the range of the auditory faculty to be heard: the sounds and voices of all devas and humans, of crawling and flying creatures, as well as the articulation of written characters; they discern the various distinctions in the wisdom expressed throughout, and are fully endowed with the power of instruction.

"The various karmas performed by sentient beings and the destinations of their merits and transgressions are seen as fruits arising from their own conduct. Observing the matters of the three periods—past, future, and present—they clearly understand the wholesome and discriminative actions of sentient beings and comprehend what they say. They recognize that all roots of virtue are fundamentally without source, without abiding, and without activity; this is what constitutes the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramitās)."
He perceives all sentient beings universally and guides them with equanimity; constantly relying upon the fundamental limit of non-self, he desires to go and meet with all people of the world.

Abiding in the world without obstruction and without pits or trenches, one attains the foremost crossing; through contemplation, one enters therein, severing all dharmas and attaining universal penetration.
He does not destroy any of the dharma-realms, for his dwelling place is the subtle and wondrous limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Should there be sentient beings amidst various sufferings and afflictions, he causes them to enter the Buddha-land and perceive all lands as being entirely the realm of humans; they attain clear vision to universally behold the ten directions and receive the holy virtues of all Buddhas.

"Having investigated the inclinations of the minds and natures of all beings, he guides and restrains them from the activities that constitute the veil of transgression; according to what he teaches and maintains, he manifests for them the accomplishment of mastery."

The path of practice one upholds accords with non-arising; it does not lack the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, or the six perfections for rescuing those in distress, leading them to the vast, expansive, and extraordinary wisdom.

The dispositions and natures of sentient beings are each diverse and different; he causes them to fulfill their respective desires and aspirations, ensuring they are free from error. He brings peace to their minds so that they may harbor joy, possessing extraordinary power without peer, and with their minds already at ease, they attain perfect enlightenment.

"Beholding with my own eyes the dispositions and conduct of sentient beings and the directions in which they incline, I shall teach and transform each according to their needs, manifesting the ultimate state so that the practices of Bodhisattvas may endure forever without interruption.
I shall cause all sentient beings to fully perfect the six pāramitās and abide in the true path, leaving nothing further to be done."
All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, have all instructed sentient beings and enabled them to attain this state:

"By making offerings to and serving the Unsurpassed Great Way, with a mind that is gentle and refined, and by approaching it with full completeness, one enables the penetration and entry into the Dharma of non-action, the wheel of the sūtra-way, all buddha-fields, and the paths of sentient beings."
All those with physical forms are enlightened and transformed; they are made pure, clear, joyful, and prevented from falling back.

With their own eyes they behold all Buddhas, making offerings to them and taking refuge in them. By means of this root of virtue, they perceive all forms as the form of a Buddha and observe all the lands of the ten directions with equanimity; thus, they are able to adorn and purify the Buddha-lands.

He thoroughly examines all devas, humans, crawling creatures, breathing beings, and the various classes of persons and things, seeing that their flattery and hypocrisy are like illusions and transformations; he fully understands this and realizes they are non-existent.
He regards the three periods of time with equanimity; in the mere instant of a single thought-moment, there is nowhere he does not enter.

Although all dharmas are each distinct and different, they are equal and without variety as they enter the power of the Way. He causes all dharmas to reach a state of singular equality, perfecting the marks and signs of mastery, and equally understanding skillful means.

He observes the minds of sentient beings and follows their inclinations and dispositions; according to their ailments, he administers the appropriate medicine, bestowing upon them equally the wisdom of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

He transcends all worldly activities, attaining purity and freshness that returns to equanimity; he washes away the afflictions, resentments, and turbidities of sentient beings' resolve, causing them to become thoroughly clear and bright.

By returning to this equanimity, one attains return to the single Dharma-body of all Buddhas and achieves its adornment; one applies oneself to this compliant Dharma, practicing its conduct with diligent vigor and earnest perseverance without slackening.

“Desiring to deliver others, by means of these roots of virtue, may all beings throughout the ten directions, at the very moment they first resolve their minds, universally attain understanding; may they explain and inform the people of the practices of all bodhisattvas, causing them all to gather together in speech, words, and meaning.”
With a single utterance, they produce countless teachings, manifesting to sentient beings the skillful means of expedient wisdom;
in the space of a single thought-moment, they cause each being to see and hear the gateways to the Path of Equality, transforming and moving them so that none fail to receive salvation.
He turns the wheel of Dharma; his tongue can cover his face and extend upward to the Brahma Heaven, and his voice is heard in distant lands.
The body of the Tathāgata manifests the gates of the Way to gladden sentient beings, and through universal peace, he emanates immeasurable and manifold rays of light.
The Buddha-way is majestic and uninterrupted; it is manifested all at once, proclaimed from the mouth throughout the ten directions and the five realms of existence.
He displays the transformations of the Buddhas so that all may dwell within them, perfecting virtuous conduct and providing instruction for the sake of all sentient beings.

Manifesting within this essence of virtue, one cultivates the gateways of immeasurable dhāraṇīs and enters into the sublime wisdom of radiant light, causing all things to be fully accomplished without exception.
"The various roots of virtue practiced by the people differ in their dispositions; [the Tathāgata] causes them to enter the wisdom of the light of *dhāraṇī*.
For all devas and all people who suffer from grief and affliction, he causes them to enter the radiance of the *dhāraṇī* to eliminate all calamities;
he causes all treatises and the ultimate limit of written characters to enter the radiance of the *dhāraṇī*."
All conditioned phenomena and all conceptualizations that are appropriate [to them] shall entirely enter the radiance of the dhāraṇī, causing them to reach the universal gate;
the revolving wheels of the sense faculties shall be made to enter the gate of the dhāraṇī-radiance;
and all adornments and pure ornaments shall be made to enter the gate of the dhāraṇī-radiance.
All paths, with their manifold excellences and majestic spiritual powers, delight all people; they enter entirely into the gate of the light of *dhāraṇī*.

Without any obstruction, they maintain all dharmas, and cause the various countless radiant splendors to be fully perfected, so that all the teachings of the Buddhas may be attained and enter into the light of *dhāraṇī*.
By virtue of these roots of merit and through these causes and conditions, they are all sustained and protected by all the Buddhas.
Regarding all Buddhas as they would their own parents, they thereby embrace Buddha-lands and cultivate them to be adorned and pure.
They are embraced by all virtuous friends and respectfully serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; with various kinds of love, joy, and delight, their minds remain unchanging and immovable.
Gathering in sentient beings and bringing their instruction to fulfillment, they protect all those in the evil realms and sever the roots of affliction through noble majesty.
Gathering in all worlds, they manifest the practice of upholding [the Dharma] and embrace the teaching of all scriptures with benevolence.
Regarding those who are to be transformed and guided, there are no dharmas to be grasped or gathered; it is because they wish to uphold and recite them.

By means of these roots of merit and through this causal retribution, they abide in a single phenomenon while universally seeing all phenomena, and abide in all phenomena while fully seeing a single phenomenon. Thus, they enter all phenomena by means of a single phenomenon, and enter a single phenomenon by means of all phenomena. They instruct and transform all meanings by means of a single meaning, and give rise to a single meaning from all meanings. Through the absence of causes and conditions, they enter into various conditions, and transform those various conditions so that they enter into the unconditioned.

By means of the dharma of non-activity, he enters into the various and distinct natures and conducts of sentient beings; following their characteristics and behaviors, he instructs them—entering into all conceptualizations by means of the absence of conceptualization, causing all who have not yet advanced to enter the Way, and entering into all states of conceptualization to guide and encourage them so that they enter the state of non-conceptualization.

"By means of these roots of virtue, for this reason, and through this auspicious response, one abides in the mental dispositions and conduct of a single sentient being and universally perceives the inclinations of all beings;
abiding in the volitions and natures of all beings, one then beholds the direction of the mind and intentions of a single person."

Ultimately perfected and vast in intention, his teaching is boundless; with the mind of a single person, he exhorts and instructs all beings regarding their intentions and thoughts, and with all minds, he gives rise to the single mind.

Then, through the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, they move and transform beings according to their needs, opening the understanding of the conduct of all sentient beings; they guide the mind of one person to enter the mental activities of all sentient beings, and by means of all minds, they encourage entry into the single mind.

He transforms the realms of sentient beings, exhorting and encouraging them while clearly manifesting the radiance of the Buddha-body; his mind dwells in the state of non-substantiality, remaining unshakable within that state of non-substantiality; he does not abandon sentient beings in the places where he establishes himself, and he attains the ultimate liberation without ever becoming weary.

“By means of these roots of virtue and through the cultivation of these matters, one dwells in a single buddha-field while universally beholding all buddha-lands; dwelling in all lands while beholding a single land; entering inexhaustible lands within all lands; and entering a single land within immeasurable lands.”

Adorning and purifying the fundamental realm of inexhaustible limits, he instructs those who enter it, severing lust, anger, and delusion so that nothing remains unscattered; dwelling in a single land, he transforms all lands, and remaining within all lands, he leads them toward a single land.

Regarding all that sentient beings conceive and contemplate, he exhorts them toward the various directions to inspire the people, causing a single buddha-field to enter into all fields, and a single land to enter into all lands, such that immeasurable buddha-fields are seen as equal to the triple world.
Because that which sentient beings initiate cannot be shaken, he transforms and guides the people through boundless compassion; yet he has no location and no place of abiding.
If they harbor doubts, he completely rescues them from hesitation, delivering all classes of sentient beings.

"By means of these roots of virtue, one enters the past through past events; furthermore, one enters the future through the past, and one enters the present through the past. One enters the future through future events; furthermore, one enters the past through future events, and future events enter the present. Furthermore, one enters the present through present events, and present events enter the past."
All that is past, future, and present enters the mark of equality; it causes the present to enter the present;
that which is present enters the past; and the past, future, and present universally enter into equality.

"By the retribution of these roots of virtue and their causal conditions, they attain the essential wisdom of the Samādhi of All Buddhas Being Present Before One’s Eyes; they reach the noble assembly of Buddha-virtues, the Right Concentration of the Tathāgata Samādhi; they attain the Samādhi of the Adornments Emanated by the Tathāgata Flower-Light; they attain the Samādhi of All-Purifying Manifestations; they attain the Samādhi of Manifesting Bodies that Display All Colors; and they enter the Samādhi of All Sounds and Languages."

Furthermore, through the manifestation of various kinds of parinirvāṇa by means of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, one attains the samādhi of the uninterrupted Buddha-teaching, and shall achieve the samādhi of exclusive purity, the samādhi of ultimate abiding, the samādhi of the adamantine site of concentration, the vajra-like samādhi, and the samādhi of the wisdom-eye.

By means of this analogy, one perceives the minds of all sentient beings; seeing that their various practices and aspirations differ, and being thoroughly proficient in all matters of the past, future, and present, this constitutes the Tathāgata’s samādhi maṇḍala.
Each shall attain distinct and diverse forms of supernatural wisdom (*abhijñā*), so that their aspirations may be fulfilled.
"By means of these roots of virtue, may I and all sentient beings achieve complete mastery over advancement and retreat, reach ultimate purity, and be graced by transformation."
By means of these roots of virtue, may the faculty of sight for all sentient beings become like the Buddha-eye;
may all sentient beings throughout the world who possess the capacity for hearing attain the Buddha-ear, so that their hearing is infinite;
and may the noses of sentient beings become like the Buddha-nose, penetrating without limit and entirely free from attachment.

May all sentient beings possess the extraordinary excellence of the faculty of the tongue, attaining the broad and long tongue of the World-Honored One; may their teachings and instructions be like the words of the Buddha;
while abiding within all worldly dharmas, may all their physical actions and undertakings be perfected as the body of a Buddha;
and while dwelling within the entire dharma-realm, may they have no fixed abode as they transform sentient beings.
All their actions constitute the karma of Buddha-wisdom; according to the inclinations and vows of the people, they transform and edify them by administering medicine according to the illness.
All fragrances can be transformed into the virtuous fragrance of the Buddha, permeating the work of the Way;
all flavors can be transformed into the flavor of the meaning of established practice; all that is subtle, smooth, and gentle enters the internal nature of people as the karma of meaning.
All dharmas are used for instruction, so as to perfect the dharma of guidance and transform sentient beings.
For all those who enter [the path], I shall cause them to achieve the great wisdom that penetrates the entryways of all Buddhas;

for the people’s veils and all their emotional afflictions, I shall raise up the Dharma to dissolve these afflictions and perform the work of a Buddha, causing all realms to become the Buddha-realm, making all faculties such that they have no [deluded] faculties, and establishing the roots of the Path for those who lack such roots.

"By means of these roots of virtue and for this reason, one attains the establishment of non-abiding wisdom; that which is the dwelling place and the foundation of the Noble Path, one causes all people to fully understand it, and transforms all forms so that they all appear in the likeness of the Buddha."

For this reason, each person was made to understand their own wisdom; all sounds and voices were transformed into the voice of a Buddha, so that they might all proclaim the Way of the Buddhas to the people.

"In this manner, causing all sentient beings to completely eliminate the gates of worldly toil and desire constitutes the bodhisattva’s entry into the gate of the dharma for practicing the path that heals others; this is the purification of the mental dispositions of all people."

It is the abode of wisdom that delights all sentient beings; it is the realm of power that enters the stage of invincibility. The practice of the bodhisattva path descends in accordance with the proper time without fail. In the actions of body, speech, and the deeds cultivated by mind, there is no obstruction, no harm, and nothing to conceal, as one proclaims the teachings of all Buddhas.
Acting without falsehood, one attains supernormal powers and fulfills all that is to be known.

By means of these roots of virtue, may my own body and all sentient beings fully achieve and reach purity; for the sake of others, I shall expound this teaching. This is the practice of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, which encourages and assists the Buddha-wisdom, remaining true and without error.

When Mañjuśrī had spoken this chapter on "Repentance with the Five Limbs," five hundred bodhisattvas all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and they all cast off their doubts, hesitations, hypocrisy, fetters, and the delusions of inverted views.
The Bodhisattva Tathāgata-samaprabha-avabhāsa attained the samādhi of all Buddhas known as "Indestructible.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, hearing from afar with his divine ear what Mañjuśrī was expounding, immediately praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
O Benevolent One, you have eloquently expounded this teaching to eliminate the obstacles and veils of all bodhisattvas and to encourage their entry into the Way.

If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this encouragement, are able to uphold, recite, and explain it, then before long they shall all extinguish every veil of sin and be rendered free from all obstructions.

It is like a lamp or a candle entering a dark room where all the gloom is dispelled; it is like the rising sun illuminating the world so that none fail to receive its light; it is like the blind regaining their sight, the deaf regaining their hearing, the mute being able to speak, the lame being able to walk, and the obstructed gaining passage.

The five aggregates naturally dissolve and the six sense-bases are extinguished; one ascends to the Hall of Dharma and enters the Chamber of the Path, surpassing the Pavilion of Wisdom to dwell in the Great Palace of the Sage.
“What is meant by the Hall of Dharma?
The Buddha said:
“It is when one’s supernormal powers are fully developed, there is no longer any obstruction, and one has attained the three types of penetrating knowledge.”
“What is meant by the ‘chamber of the Way’?
The Buddha said:

“Attaining the concentration of samādhi, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions as clearly as a person looking into a mirror; there is no distance between them, and they are seen everywhere and in their entirety.”
“What is meant by the ‘platform of wisdom’?
The Buddha said:
“It is the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), which understands that all things are empty, remains free from attachment in the mind, and possesses great kindness and great compassion.”
“What is meant by the ‘Great Hall’?
The Buddha said:

“It is skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), knowing the proper time for advancing or retreating; it does not abide in the conditioned (saṃskṛta) nor dwell in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); it is united with the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), without union and without dispersal.”

Manifesting forms within the three realms, he transforms into the body of a Buddha; with his marks and embellishments and majestic countenance, he proclaims the Way and its teachings. At times he appears as a Bodhisattva, a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha, a noble man, a great sage, or an ordinary person of foolish conduct; according to the occasion, he opens the way for transformation and delivers beings throughout the ten directions, so that none fail to attain salvation and reach the Great Way.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Equal Radiance, the Venerable Ānanda, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and the people of the world were all filled with joy; they paid homage and withdrew.
